analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated federal trust fund for water and sewer repairs, funded by a higher corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 100 House Democratic cosponsors but was never given a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a dedicated Water Affordability, Transparency, Equity, and Reliability Trust Fund, bankrolled by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%. The money would flow to state revolving loan funds for clean water and drinking water, lead pipe removal in schools, PFAS filtration for contaminated wells, tribal and border-community water projects, and training for water-plant workers. It also steers most of that aid to publicly owned water systems and lets municipalities buy private water utilities from willing or unwilling sellers. It died without any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Households struggling with rising water and sewer bills, families with lead pipes or contaminated wells, schools replacing lead fountains, tribal communities and border colonias lacking safe water, and low-income workers trained for water-system jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households facing high water bills and contamination

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated trust fund — capped at the larger of $35 billion a year or a share of EPA's 20-year water-need estimates — so water and sewer repairs get a guaranteed funding stream instead of competing in yearly budget fights [S3].
Raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5% to pay for the fund, with the revenue automatically transferred to it [S2] [S3].

Directs most of the money to the clean water and drinking water state revolving loan funds (42% each) and expands eligibility to include replacing lead service lines with grants to property owners, upgrading treatment plants to handle PFAS contamination, and filtering contaminated household wells [S3].

Raises school drinking-water infrastructure grants from $5 million to $1.05 billion a year through 2025 to make school fountains, coolers, and filling stations lead-free, and expands tribal drinking water funding from 1.5% to 3% of revolving fund grants [S3].

Funds job training — apprenticeships and pre-apprenticeships — for water and wastewater operator jobs, with at least half the grants reserved for low- and very low-income workers, including those in high-poverty and heavily minority ZIP codes [S3].

Requires states to let federally funded water projects use project labor agreements and keeps prevailing-wage rules in place, and creates a $100 million-a-year program for water and sewer aid to colonias along the border [S3].

Steers aid toward publicly owned, operated, and managed water systems and allows municipalities to purchase privately owned water utilities — even from an unwilling seller — using revolving-fund money [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations pay through a 3.5-point higher corporate tax rate; investor-owned water utilities face the loss of public subsidies and possible municipal buyouts; general taxpayers eventually bear the cost of the expanded grant programs.

drawbacks.text: Raising the corporate rate from 21% to 24.5% reverses a major piece of the 2017 tax law, and critics argued it would raise costs for businesses and reduce investment; the bill includes no offsetting spending cuts [S2] [S3].

The bill channels aid to publicly owned systems and lets towns condemn and buy private water utilities, which private operators said would discourage the investment they make in systems, particularly for small towns that rely on them — though the bill exempts systems serving fewer than 10,000 people [S3].

The trust fund is set up to be self-funded from the tax increase rather than subject to annual appropriations, which supporters see as stability and fiscal skeptics see as automatic spending insulated from yearly budget review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackles a real and expensive problem — EPA's own surveys put 20-year water infrastructure needs in the hundreds of billions — and pays for it with a dedicated corporate tax increase rather than adding to the deficit. The trade-off is genuinely contested: who should bear the cost (corporate shareholders) and who should own the water systems (public entities versus private utilities) are legitimate policy disagreements, not loopholes. Its main practical weakness was political: it drew no Republican support, so it had no path in a Republican-run House.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and three of their subcommittees, but none ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill on March 22, 2023, with 67 original cosponsors [S1] [S3].

It was referred to six committees — Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Agriculture, Natural Resources, and Education and the Workforce — a multi-committee referral that made consideration harder to coordinate [S1] [S5].
Within days it was sent to subcommittees on water resources, environment, and commodity markets, but no markup, hearing, or vote ever followed [S5].
Cosponsorship grew to 100 members — all Democrats — but no Republican ever cosponsored it [S4].
The bill never reached the House floor and expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: House Republicans and the corporate and private-utility interests that would have paid for the fund — the corporate tax rate stayed at 21%, private water utilities kept their business and public subsidies untouched, and no water-infrastructure money flowed. Households facing rising water bills, lead pipes, and PFAS contamination got nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 100 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run House never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill bars revolving-fund aid from supporting private systems, requires most aid go to publicly owned systems, and lets municipalities buy private water utilities even from an unwilling seller. This would shrink private utilities' markets and remove public subsidies that currently flow to them.
A 3.5-point higher corporate income tax funds the trust fund, directly costing corporations and shareholders to pay for water infrastructure and household affordability programs.

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction contractors and building-trades unions
industries.note: The bill requires federally funded water projects to use project labor agreements and preserves prevailing-wage rules, steering construction work toward union-signatory contractors and creating a jobs-training pipeline for water-plant operators.

The fund's largest allocations — 42% each to the clean water and drinking water state revolving funds — flow through public systems, which become the required channel for the new aid, locking in public ownership as the model for water service.
